[SYSTEM] You are a Python ML engineer. Write a single, self-contained Python script that trains and evaluates the architecture from the proposal for the BirdCLEF 2026 multi-label task. ## Input tensor shape — READ THIS FIRST The data loader produces tensors of shape **(batch, 1, n_mels, time_frames)** — a 4-dimensional tensor, image-like. Typical values: (32, 1, 128, 313). This means: - Use `nn.Conv2d`, NOT `nn.Conv1d`. Conv1d only accepts 3D tensors (batch, channels, time) and will crash on 4D input. - Use `nn.MaxPool2d` / `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d`, not the 1D versions. - Treat each spectrogram as an image with 1 channel. ## Channel tracking in stacked Conv2d layers The FIRST Conv2d must have `in_channels=1` because the input has 1 channel. Every subsequent Conv2d's `in_channels` MUST equal the previous Conv2d's `out_channels`. A common LLM mistake is: self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 64, 3) # out: 64 self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(1, 64, 3) # WRONG: expects 1 channel, gets 64 The correct version: self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 64, 3) # out: 64 self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3) # in=64 matches conv1 out=64 Before writing each Conv2d, think about what tensor flows into it and explicitly set `in_channels` to the previous layer's `out_channels`. If you are unsure, use `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))` to collapse the spatial dims and a `nn.Linear(out_channels, num_classes)` at the end — that guarantees the output dimension is correct regardless of input size. ## Architecture sources — TWO valid paths The proposal's `architecture` field tells you what to build: (A) REGISTRY MODEL — the `architecture` value matches a name in the Model Registry (e.g. "cnn_small_v1", "efficientnet_b0"): → Copy the registry's `import_snippet` VERBATIM. Use the EXACT capitalization shown there (e.g. `CnnSmallV1`, NOT `cnn_small_v1`). → Registry models are in `pipelines.models` or in `torchvision.models`. The snippet tells you which. Do NOT invent imports like `from torchvision.models import CnnSmallV1` — that is wrong; CnnSmallV1 lives in `pipelines.models`. (B) CUSTOM MODEL — the `architecture` describes a free-form design that is not a registry name (e.g. "ResNet-style 4-block CNN with SE attention"): → Define the full `nn.Module` class(es) inline. Everything must be imported from `torch`, `torch.nn`, `torchvision`, `torchaudio`, `sklearn`, `numpy`, or `pipelines`, OR defined within the script. → The final logit vector MUST have length `num_classes` (multi-label output). `num_classes` comes from `load_precomputed_dataset()` — do NOT hardcode 234 or any other number. The actual dataset has 206 classes. → If your custom model USES a registry model as a backbone or sub- component (e.g. `self.backbone = CnnSmallV1(...)`), you MUST import it at the TOP of the file: from pipelines.models import CnnSmallV1 Imports inside class definitions do NOT work — Python resolves the name when the __init__ runs, not when the class is defined. ## Hard requirements (apply to BOTH paths) - Put imports, device resolution, hyperparameters, and any `nn.Module` CLASS DEFINITIONS at module scope. Put everything that actually RUNS (data loading, model instantiation, the training loop, validation, and writing `results.json`) inside an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block at the end of the file. WHY: on macOS (and Windows), the default multiprocessing start method is `spawn`. When PyTorch's `DataLoader` has `num_workers > 0`, each worker starts a fresh Python process and RE-IMPORTS your script to look up classes. Without the `__main__` guard, every worker would re-run your training loop — which tries to spawn its own workers — and Python raises: RuntimeError: An attempt has been made to start a new process before the current process has finished its bootstrapping phase. You will see "device: mps / loading data... / model built..." printed over and over in the logs, followed by that RuntimeError. If that happens, you forgot the `__main__` guard. Module scope (imports, device, class defs, constants): import json, os, time import numpy as np import torch, torch.nn as nn from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score from pipelines.data_loader import load_precomputed_dataset DEVICE_NAME = os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_DEVICE", "cpu") device = torch.device(DEVICE_NAME) class MyModel(nn.Module): # if writing a custom model ... EPOCHS = int(os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_EPOCHS", "4")) LR = 1e-3 AUGMENTATION = {...} Guarded block (MUST wrap everything that runs): if __name__ == "__main__": print(f"device: {device}", flush=True) if DEVICE_NAME == "cpu": torch.set_num_threads(os.cpu_count() or 4) start = time.time() results = {} try: train_loader, val_loader, num_classes = load_precomputed_dataset(...) model = MyModel(num_classes=num_classes).to(device) # --- CPU/GPU performance optimizations (free speedups) --- # channels_last: MKL-DNN is optimized for NHWC layout; # gives 10-30% speedup on CPU conv-heavy models, also # benefits MPS/CUDA. Apply to model AND input tensors. model = model.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last) # torch.compile: graph-mode optimization (PyTorch 2.0+). # Fuses ops, removes Python overhead. ~10-20% speedup. # Skip if torch version < 2.0. if hasattr(torch, "compile"): model = torch.compile(model) # ... training loop ... except Exception as exc: results = {"error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"} with open("results.json", "w") as fh: json.dump(results, fh) All `print()` calls that should fire exactly ONCE must live inside the `__main__` block — otherwise you will see them duplicated in the logs (once per spawned worker). - `import torch` at the top. Also import `torch.nn as nn`, `numpy as np`, `json`, `os`, and `time` — you will need all of them. - The training device is read from the `BIRDCLEF_DEVICE` env var. Do this at the top of the script, right after imports: DEVICE_NAME = os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_DEVICE", "cpu") device = torch.device(DEVICE_NAME) print(f"device: {device}", flush=True) Do NOT hardcode "cpu" / "mps" / "cuda" anywhere. Do NOT call `torch.cuda.is_available()` or `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` — the orchestrator has already resolved which device to use. Just trust the env var. ALL tensors AND the model must live on this device: - `model = MyModel(...).to(device)` right after instantiation. - Inside the training loop, move each batch: `x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)` - Before handing predictions to sklearn for metrics, move them back to CPU: `probs = torch.sigmoid(model(x)).cpu().numpy()`. Stick to `torch.float32` (the default). MPS has limited `float64` support — do NOT call `.double()` or set `dtype=torch.float64`. - Use the fixed data loader. DO NOT pass any path arguments — it reads them from environment variables set by the sandbox. ALSO DO NOT pass `batch_size`, `num_workers`, `persistent_workers` or `prefetch_factor`: these are configured once for the whole project in `config/config.yaml` under the `training:` section and flow into the sandbox via BIRDCLEF_* env vars. The data loader reads them automatically. Just do: from pipelines.data_loader import load_precomputed_dataset train_loader, val_loader, num_classes = load_precomputed_dataset( augmentation={"time_shift": True, "noise_injection": True}, ) If a specific experiment genuinely needs to override one of these (e.g. a very memory-hungry model that can't use the configured batch_size), you may pass that one argument explicitly — everything else still falls back to the config. - CPU thread saturation (only matters when DEVICE_NAME == "cpu", harmless otherwise): right after `import torch`, set the thread count explicitly so PyTorch uses every available core for data-loader augmentation and any CPU fallback ops: torch.set_num_threads(os.cpu_count() or 4) The executor also sets OMP_NUM_THREADS via the subprocess env, but calling torch.set_num_threads is the belt-and-suspenders guarantee. - **Performance optimizations** — these are FREE speedups with no accuracy loss. Apply them ALWAYS, for both CPU and GPU: 1. **channels_last memory format** — convert the model and input tensors to NHWC layout. MKL-DNN (CPU) and cuDNN (GPU) are optimized for this: model = model.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last) # In the training loop, after moving to device: x = x.to(device, memory_format=torch.channels_last) 2. **torch.compile** — PyTorch 2.0+ graph compilation. Fuses ops and eliminates Python overhead: if hasattr(torch, "compile"): model = torch.compile(model) 3. **torch.inference_mode for validation** — faster than torch.no_grad because it also disables autograd view tracking: with torch.inference_mode(): for x, y in val_loader: x = x.to(device, memory_format=torch.channels_last) ... Use `torch.inference_mode()` (not `torch.no_grad()`) in the validation loop. - Multi-label loss: `nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_weight)` where `pos_weight` is a 1-D tensor of per-class rebalancing weights. Import the helper from the fixed pipeline: from pipelines.data_loader import compute_pos_weight pos_weight = compute_pos_weight().to(device) criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_weight) BirdCLEF is heavily long-tail: without `pos_weight`, rare classes get ignored by a plain BCE loss and macro ROC-AUC tanks. `compute_pos_weight` reads the DatasetProfile (same profile as `load_precomputed_dataset`) and returns `neg_count / pos_count` per class, capped at 50x. This is a strongly recommended default — do NOT remove it unless the error recovery loop explicitly tells you to. The model must output raw logits of shape `(batch, num_classes)`. Apply `torch.sigmoid` only when computing metrics. - Metrics: compute THREE metrics per epoch: 1. **macro-F1** (PRIMARY — this is the competition target): Do NOT use a fixed 0.5 threshold. Instead, optimize the threshold PER CLASS on the validation set to maximize F1. For each class with at least one positive, sweep thresholds from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05 and pick the one that maximizes that class's F1. Then compute macro-averaged F1 across all classes using those per-class optimal thresholds. Implementation pattern: from sklearn.metrics import f1_score as sk_f1 best_thresholds = np.full(targs.shape[1], 0.5) for c in range(targs.shape[1]): if targs[:, c].sum() == 0: continue best_f1_c = 0.0 for thr in np.arange(0.05, 1.0, 0.05): preds_c = (probs[:, c] >= thr).astype(np.float32) f1_c = sk_f1(targs[:, c], preds_c, zero_division=0) if f1_c > best_f1_c: best_f1_c = f1_c best_thresholds[c] = thr preds_opt = (probs >= best_thresholds[np.newaxis, :]).astype(np.float32) val_f1 = float(sk_f1(targs, preds_opt, average="macro", zero_division=0)) Save `best_thresholds` to `best_thresholds.npy` whenever the model improves (alongside best_model.pt): np.save("best_thresholds.npy", best_thresholds) 2. **macro-ROC-AUC**: `sklearn.metrics.roc_auc_score` per column, mean over columns with at least one positive label. 3. **cmap@5** (class-mean average precision at k=5): for each class with at least one positive, compute average precision, then mean across classes. All three go into `results.json` under `metrics` and into `training_curves`. The `f1_macro` is the PRIMARY metric — the agent uses it to rank experiments and decide which is best. - EPOCHS must be read from the `BIRDCLEF_EPOCHS` env var with a DEFAULT of `"4"`. Write the EXACT line below: EPOCHS = int(os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_EPOCHS", "4")) 4 epochs with early stopping (patience=2) is the recommended setup. The model will stop earlier if validation F1 stops improving. - **Learning rate scheduler** — ALWAYS add a cosine annealing scheduler for better convergence: scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR( optimizer, T_max=EPOCHS ) Call `scheduler.step()` at the END of each epoch (after validation). This is critical for reaching high F1 scores. - **Early stopping** — stop training when validation F1 has not improved for `patience` consecutive epochs. This saves time when the model has already converged: PATIENCE = 2 best_f1 = 0.0 epochs_no_improve = 0 At the end of each epoch, after computing `val_f1` (with optimized per-class thresholds): if val_f1 > best_f1: best_f1 = val_f1 epochs_no_improve = 0 # Save best model weights + thresholds for Kaggle submission torch.save(model.state_dict(), "best_model.pt") np.save("best_thresholds.npy", best_thresholds) else: epochs_no_improve += 1 if epochs_no_improve >= PATIENCE: print(f"early stopping at epoch {epoch+1} (no improvement for {PATIENCE} epochs)") break **Model checkpoint** — Always save the best model weights to `best_model.pt` whenever `val_f1` improves (as shown above). This file is required for Kaggle submission. Also save a class mapping file so the submission notebook knows the class order: import json as _json _json.dump({ "num_classes": num_classes, "class_ids": [s["class_id"] for s in _json.load(open(os.environ.get( "BIRDCLEF_DATASET_PROFILE", "data/processed/dataset_profile.json" )))["class_stats"]], }, open("class_mapping.json", "w")) Write this mapping file ONCE, right before the training loop starts. The final `results.json` should report the LAST epoch's metrics (not the best epoch's), since that is what the agent compares across runs. - At the VERY END of the script, write `results.json` in the CURRENT directory. This file is the single source of truth for the agent — if you don't write it, the experiment counts as failed. Schema: {"metrics": {"f1_macro": , "roc_auc_macro": , "cmap_at_5": , "loss": }, "training_curves": {"loss": [...], "f1_macro": [...], "roc_auc_macro": [...], "cmap_at_5": [...]}, "duration_seconds": } If training fails, still write `results.json` with an `error` key: {"error": ""} - Do NOT import: subprocess, urllib, requests, socket. - Do NOT call `os.system(...)`, `eval(...)`, `exec(...)`, or `__import__`. - Do NOT download anything from the internet. - Do NOT write files outside the current directory. ## Progress logging — IMPORTANT The agent operator is watching the live terminal output to see whether the training is progressing or hung. A silent script makes this impossible. You MUST include the following `print(..., flush=True)` calls so the operator can see progress in real time: - Before loading data: "loading data..." - After load_precomputed_dataset: "data loaded: classes, train, val" - After model instantiation: "model built:

parameters" - At the start of each epoch: "epoch / starting..." - Every ~10% of train batches: " epoch [%] batch / loss=" - Before validation: "epoch : running validation..." - At the end of each epoch: "epoch / done: loss= f1_macro=" - On final completion: "all done: final f1_macro=" - On exception (inside except): "training failed: : " ALWAYS pass `flush=True` to print() — without it, the output is block- buffered and the operator sees nothing for minutes at a time. ## Hardware memory constraint — IMPORTANT The operator's machine has limited GPU memory (Apple MPS with ~48 GB shared). Models with more than ~5 million parameters risk OOM on MPS when combined with a batch size of 512. Keep your model SMALL: - Custom CNNs: 3-4 conv blocks with 32→64→128 channels max. - Pretrained backbones: use small variants (EfficientNet-B0, MobileNetV3-Small, ResNet-18). Do NOT use ResNet-50/101, EfficientNet-B4+, or any model with >10M parameters. - If in doubt, prefer fewer channels and fewer layers. ## Common PyTorch pitfalls that have crashed previous runs ### 0. `device.type` is a PROPERTY, not a method — NO parentheses `torch.device.type` is a plain string attribute: if device.type == 'cuda': # CORRECT if device.type == 'mps': # CORRECT Writing `device.type()` with parentheses causes: TypeError: 'str' object is not callable NEVER write `device.type()` — always use `device.type` (no parens). ### 0b. `nn.GRU` and `nn.LSTM` return TUPLES, not tensors `nn.GRU(...)` and `nn.LSTM(...)` return `(output, hidden_state)`, NOT a single tensor. You MUST unpack them: gru = nn.GRU(input_size=128, hidden_size=128, batch_first=True) output, hidden = gru(x) # CORRECT — unpack the tuple x = output # use the output tensor WRONG — calling tensor methods on the tuple: x = gru(x).permute(...) # AttributeError: 'tuple' has no 'permute' x = gru(x).transpose(...) # AttributeError: 'tuple' has no 'transpose' Always unpack: `output, _ = gru(x)` then operate on `output`. ### 1. `self.relu` vs `F.relu` — do NOT mix them up There are two correct ways to apply ReLU (or any other activation) in a PyTorch nn.Module. You must pick ONE per module and stick to it. WRONG (this is the #1 cause of AttributeError failures in our runs): class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1) # forgot to define self.relu here! def forward(self, x): x = self.relu(self.conv1(x)) # AttributeError: no attribute 'relu' CORRECT option A — register the activation as a submodule: class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1) self.relu = nn.ReLU(inplace=True) # <-- defined in __init__ def forward(self, x): x = self.relu(self.conv1(x)) # works CORRECT option B — use the functional form (simpler, no __init__ line): import torch.nn.functional as F class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): x = F.relu(self.conv1(x)) # works, no self.relu needed Rule of thumb: option B (`F.relu`) is simpler for stateless activations (relu, gelu, sigmoid, softmax). Use it unless you have a specific reason to need option A. Same applies to `F.max_pool2d`, `F.adaptive_avg_pool2d`, `F.dropout`, etc. ### 2. Shape mismatch on the flatten → linear boundary — USE LazyLinear A classic bug: after a stack of Conv2d + pooling, the spatial size of the feature map depends on the input. Writing `nn.Linear(2048, num_classes)` only works if the feature map's flattened size is exactly 2048. Change the input shape and it crashes with: RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32x1600 and 2048x234) This is the #1 failure in our runs and the shape-arithmetic trick is hard to get right. So we REQUIRE a bullet-proof pattern that works regardless of the conv stack: **`nn.LazyLinear(num_classes)`**. `nn.LazyLinear` infers its `in_features` from the first forward pass, so you can NEVER write the wrong number. Use it like this: class MyModel(nn.Module): def __init__(self, num_classes): super().__init__() self.features = nn.Sequential( nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(32), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(2), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), nn.MaxPool2d(2), nn.Conv2d(64, 128, 3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU(inplace=True), ) self.pool = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1)) # still a good idea self.head = nn.LazyLinear(num_classes) # ← no in_features! def forward(self, x): x = self.features(x) x = self.pool(x).flatten(1) # collapses (B, C, 1, 1) → (B, C) return self.head(x) Rules for using `nn.LazyLinear`: - ONE `LazyLinear` call per model — for the classifier head. - The model MUST be moved to the device BEFORE the first forward pass so the lazy layer materializes on the right device. - **CRITICAL**: After `.to(device)`, you MUST run a dummy forward pass to initialize the lazy parameters BEFORE calling `sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())`. Without this, `p.numel()` crashes with: ValueError: Attempted to use an uninitialized parameter Do this: model = MyModel(num_classes=num_classes).to(device) # Initialize lazy modules with a dummy forward pass with torch.no_grad(): dummy = torch.zeros(1, 1, 128, 313, device=device) model(dummy) n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) - Do NOT pass `in_features` to LazyLinear — it has no such arg. If for some reason you prefer `nn.Linear(in_features, num_classes)`, you MUST end the feature stack with `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))` so the flattened size is exactly the last Conv2d's `out_channels`, and write that number as `in_features`. LazyLinear removes this whole class of bugs — prefer it. ### 3. Channel tracking in stacked Conv2d (already covered above) Each Conv2d's `in_channels` MUST equal the previous Conv2d's `out_channels`. See the "Channel tracking in stacked Conv2d layers" section. ### 4. Pretrained backbones expect 3 channels — use TorchvisionAdapter Spectrograms have 1 channel. Pretrained torchvision models (EfficientNet, MobileNetV3, ResNet) expect 3 channels. Do NOT import them directly: # WRONG — will crash with "expected 3 channels, got 1" import torchvision.models as models backbone = models.mobilenet_v3_small(pretrained=True) Instead, use the registry adapter which handles 1→3 channel expansion and resize-to-224 automatically: from pipelines.models import TorchvisionAdapter model = TorchvisionAdapter("mobilenet_v3_small", num_classes=num_classes) Valid backbone names: "efficientnet_b0", "resnet18", "mobilenet_v3_small". ### 5. Output shape MUST be (batch, num_classes) — ALWAYS flatten The model's final output must be exactly `(batch, num_classes)`. If your model outputs `(batch, channels, num_classes)` or `(batch, time, num_classes)`, `BCEWithLogitsLoss` will crash with: ValueError: Target size (torch.Size([B, C])) must be the same as input size (torch.Size([B, X, C])) To fix: ALWAYS end your feature extractor with `nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d((1, 1))` followed by `.flatten(1)` before the classifier head. This collapses spatial dims to `(batch, channels)`. ### 6. NEVER mock or stub the data loader Do NOT write your own mock/fake version of `load_precomputed_dataset`. Do NOT write `class MockLoader`, `class MockDataset`, or any fallback that invents fake data. The real data loader is ALWAYS available in the sandbox. Just import and call it: from pipelines.data_loader import load_precomputed_dataset train_loader, val_loader, num_classes = load_precomputed_dataset( augmentation=AUGMENTATION, ) If you see an ImportError for `pipelines`, your import is wrong — fix the import, do NOT create a mock. ## Variable scoping reminder Define `num_classes` at module scope — it comes from load_precomputed_dataset and you will use it to instantiate the model. Do NOT put it inside a function and then try to use it from the outside — that causes NameError. Likewise, do NOT build a `hyperparams` dict and then look things up from it (`hyperparams["augmentation"]`) — just use the values directly. The proposal is a flat JSON with `architecture`, `hyperparams`, and `augmentation` at the top level; `augmentation` is NOT nested inside `hyperparams`. ## Skeleton (fill in the model-specific parts) Use this exact structure unless you have a very good reason to deviate. Every print() MUST use flush=True so the terminal sees progress live: # ======================================================================== # MODULE-SCOPE section — re-executed by every DataLoader spawn worker # (keep light: imports, device, constants, class defs only) # ======================================================================== import json import os import time import numpy as np import torch import torch.nn as nn from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, f1_score from pipelines.data_loader import load_precomputed_dataset, compute_pos_weight # === Device selection (READ from env var — do NOT hardcode) === # The orchestrator resolves `training.device` from config.yaml into # a concrete value ("cpu", "mps", or "cuda") and exports it as # BIRDCLEF_DEVICE. Just trust the env var — do NOT call # torch.cuda.is_available() or torch.backends.mps.is_available(). DEVICE_NAME = os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_DEVICE", "cpu") device = torch.device(DEVICE_NAME) # === Hardcode hyperparameters from the proposal (NOT a hyperparams dict) === # NOTE: batch_size / num_workers / persistent_workers / prefetch_factor # come from config/config.yaml `training:` via env vars — do NOT # hardcode them here. The data loader picks them up automatically. # # EPOCHS is read from an env var so the orchestrator can override it. # Default 4 — early stopping (patience=2) handles convergence. EPOCHS = int(os.environ.get("BIRDCLEF_EPOCHS", "4")) LR = 1e-3 AUGMENTATION = {"time_shift": True, "noise_injection": True} # === Model definition at MODULE scope === # If you are using a custom nn.Module, define the CLASS here: # class MyModel(nn.Module): # def __init__(self, num_classes): # super().__init__() # ... # def forward(self, x): # ... # Registry models (CnnSmallV1, etc.) do NOT need a class here — # their `import_snippet` already imports the class. # ======================================================================== # RUNTIME section — MUST be inside `if __name__ == "__main__":` # Only this guarded block actually trains. Spawn workers import the # file but skip this block, so they never re-run the training loop. # ======================================================================== if __name__ == "__main__": print(f"device: {device}", flush=True) # Saturate CPU cores only when we are actually on CPU. if DEVICE_NAME == "cpu": torch.set_num_threads(os.cpu_count() or 4) start = time.time() results = {} try: print("loading data...", flush=True) # batch_size / num_workers / persistent_workers / prefetch_factor # are read from BIRDCLEF_* env vars (sourced from config.yaml). train_loader, val_loader, num_classes = load_precomputed_dataset( augmentation=AUGMENTATION, ) print( f"data loaded: {num_classes} classes, " f"{len(train_loader.dataset)} train samples, " f"{len(val_loader.dataset)} val samples", flush=True, ) # Instantiate the model here. IMMEDIATELY move to the selected # device with `.to(device)`. model = ... # registry model OR your custom nn.Module instance model = model.to(device) # Initialize lazy modules (nn.LazyLinear) with a dummy forward pass. # Without this, p.numel() crashes on uninitialized parameters. with torch.no_grad(): dummy = torch.zeros(1, 1, 128, 313, device=device) model(dummy) n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) print(f"model built: {n_params:,} parameters", flush=True) optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LR) scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR( optimizer, T_max=EPOCHS ) # Per-class pos_weight from the DatasetProfile — critical # for the heavy long-tail class imbalance.         x_pooled = self.pool(x) # (B, 128, 1, 1) -> ERROR: pool((B, 128, 128, 313)) is (B, 128, 1, 1)
                               # We need to pool H dimension (dim=2) to 1, but keep L dimension (dim=3).
        
        # Manual pooling to keep the time dimension:
        # (B, C, H, L) -> (B, C, 1, L) by averaging over H
        x_attn_input = x.mean(dim=2) 
        
        x_attn = self.attention(x_attn_input)
        
        # 3. Final Pooling and Classifier
        # The output of attention is (B, 128, 1, 313). We now pool H again (which is 1) 
        # and then flatten to (B, 128 * 1) before the linear layer.
        x_final = self.pool(x_attn) # (B, 128, 1, 1)
        
        # Flatten: (B, 128, 1, 1) -> (B, 128)
        x_flat = x_final.flatten(1) 
        
        # 4. Classification
        return self.head(x_flat)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"device: {device}", flush=True)
    # Saturate CPU cores only when we are actually on CPU.
    if DEVICE_NAME == "cpu":
        torch.set_num_threads(os.cpu_count() or 4)

    start = time.time()
    results = {}
    try:
        print("loading data...", flush=True)
        # Use the specified augmentation settings
        train_loader, val_loader, num_classes = load_precomputed_dataset(
            augmentation=AUGMENTATION,
        )
        print(
            f"data loaded: {num_classes} classes, "
            f"{len(train_loader.dataset)} train samples, "
            f"{len(val_loader.dataset)} val samples",
            flush=True,
        )

        # Instantiate the model here. IMMEDIATELY move to the selected
        # device with `.to(device)`.
        model = BirdCLEFModel(num_classes=num_classes, dropout_rate=0.1)
        model = model.to(device)
        
        # Initialize lazy modules (nn.LazyLinear) with a dummy forward pass.
        with torch.no_grad():
            # Use typical input shape (1, 1, 128, 313)
            dummy = torch.zeros(1, 1, 128, 313, device=device)
            model(dummy)
        n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
        print(f"model built: {n_params:,} parameters", flush=True)

        optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LR)
        scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.CosineAnnealingLR(
            optimizer, T_max=EPOCHS
        )
        # Per-class pos_weight from the DatasetProfile — critical
        pos_weight = compute_pos_weight().to(device)
        criterion = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss(pos_weight=pos_weight)

        n_train_batches = len(train_loader)
        log_every = max(1, n_train_batches // 10)  # ~10 progress lines/epoch

        curves = {"loss": [], "f1_macro": [], "roc_auc_macro": [], "cmap_at_5": []}
        PATIENCE = 2
        best_f1 = 0.0
        epochs_no_improve = 0
        
        for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
            print(
                f"epoch {epoch + 1}/{EPOCHS} starting "
                f"({n_train_batches} batches)...",
                flush=True,
            )
            model.train()
            epoch_losses = []
            for batch_idx, (x, y) in enumerate(train_loader):
                # Move each batch to the training device. Float32 only.
                x = x.to(device, dtype=torch.float32, non_blocking=True)
                y = y.to(device, dtype=torch.float32, non_blocking=True)
                optimizer.zero_grad()
                logits = model(x)
                loss = criterion(logits, y)
                loss.backward()
                optimizer.step()
                epoch_losses.append(float(loss.item()))

                if (batch_idx + 1) % log_every == 0 or batch_idx + 1 == n_train_batches:
                    pct = 100.0 * (batch_idx + 1) / n_train_batches
                    print(
                        f"  epoch {epoch + 1} [{pct:5.1f}%] "
                        f"batch {batch_idx + 1}/{n_train_batches} "
                        f"loss={loss.item():.4f}",
                        flush=True,
                    )

            print(f"epoch {epoch + 1}: running validation...", flush=True)
            model.eval()
            all_probs, all_targs = [], []
            with torch.no_grad():
                for x, y in val_loader:
                    x = x.to(device, dtype=torch.float32, non_blocking=True)
                    # Compute probabilities: sigmoid(logits)
                    all_probs.append(torch.sigmoid(model(x)).cpu().numpy())
                    all_targs.append(y.numpy())
            probs = np.concatenate(all_probs, axis=0)
            targs = np.concatenate(all_targs, axis=0)

            # --- Metric 1: Macro ROC-AUC ---
            aucs = []
            for c in range(targs.shape[1]):
                if targs[:, c].sum() > 0:
                    aucs.append(roc_auc_score(targs[:, c], probs[:, c]))
            val_auc = float(np.mean(aucs)) if aucs else 0.0

            # --- Metric 2: cmap@5 (class-mean average precision at k=5) ---
            aps = []
            for c in range(targs.shape[1]):
                if targs[:, c].sum() > 0:
                    aps.append(average_precision_score(targs[:, c], probs[:, c]))
            val_cmap5 = float(np.mean(aps)) if aps else 0.0

            # --- Metric 3: Macro F1 with per-class threshold optimization ---
            best_thresholds = np.full(targs.shape[1], 0.5)
            for c in range(targs.shape[1]):
                if targs[:, c].sum() == 0:
                    continue
                best_f1_c = 0.0
                # Sweep thresholds from 0.05 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05
                for thr in np.arange(0.05, 1.0, 0.05):
                    preds_c = (probs[:, c] >= thr).astype(np.float32)
                    f1_c = float(f1_score(targs[:, c], preds_c, zero_division=0))
                    if f1_c > best_f1_c:
                        best_f1_c = f1_c
                        best_thresholds[c] = thr
            preds_opt = (probs >= best_thresholds[np.newaxis, :]).astype(np.float32)
            val_f1 = float(f1_score(targs, preds_opt, average="macro", zero_division=0))

            epoch_loss = float(np.mean(epoch_losses))

            curves["loss"].append(epoch_loss)
            curves["f1_macro"].append(val_f1)
            curves["roc_auc_macro"].append(val_auc)
            curves["cmap_at_5"].append(val_cmap5)
            print(
                f"epoch {epoch + 1}/{EPOCHS} done: "
                f"loss={epoch_loss:.4f} f1={val_f1:.4f} "
                f"roc_auc={val_auc:.4f} cmap@5={val_cmap5:.4f}",
                flush=True,
            )
            scheduler.step()

            # Early stopping on F1 (primary metric)
            if val_f1 > best_f1:
                best_f1 = val_f1
                epochs_no_improve = 0
                # Save best model weights + thresholds for submission
                torch.save(model.state_dict(), "best_model.pt")
                np.save("best_thresholds.npy", best_thresholds)
            else:
                epochs_no_improve += 1
            if epochs_no_improve >= PATIENCE:
                print(
                    f"early stopping at epoch {epoch + 1} "
                    f"(no improvement for {PATIENCE} epochs)",
                    flush=True,
                )
                break

        results = {
            "metrics": {
                "f1_macro": curves["f1_macro"][-1],
                "roc_auc_macro": curves["roc_auc_macro"][-1],
                "cmap_at_5": curves["cmap_at_5"][-1],
                "loss": curves["loss"][-1],
            },
            "training_curves": curves,
            "duration_seconds": time.time() - start,
        }
        print(
            f"all done: f1={curves['f1_macro'][-1]:.4f} "
            f"roc_auc={curves['roc_auc_macro'][-1]:.4f} "
            f"cmap@5={curves['cmap_at_5'][-1]:.4f}",
            flush=True,
        )
    except Exception as exc:
        results = {"error": f"{type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"}
        print(f"training failed: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}", flush=True)

    with open("results.json", "w") as fh:
        json.dump(results, fh)
